quote:
It was just everything I ever got in my life was just pure fight and pure drive.
There wasn't any luck towards it. It was more like the harder I worked, the luckier I got.
label: investor_experience_bias
interpretation: Hyatt attributes his own outcomes to sustained effort and drive, suggesting that his operating history may shape how he thinks about entrepreneurial persistence; this is personal history, not an explicit investment criterion.

quote:
What I learned in business was that, you know, there was never a time, there was never a
contract, there was never one thing that made us great or really big.
There was just these very small little bullets and there was never one big cannonball.
label: founder_execution
interpretation: His operating lesson favors cumulative, consistent execution over dependence on a single breakthrough event, but it is not stated as a formal investing rule.

quote:
Often, some of you are starting companies and if you could just sign AT&T or you just sign
this big client, it's all going to be a panacea of goodness.
That's not true.
label: traction_repeatability_concern
interpretation: Hyatt cautions founders against treating one major customer win as sufficient evidence of durable success, implying concern about traction that depends on a single event.

quote:
Success is very, very small things.
You hired a great employee.
You did this.
You made a little bit of revenue.
Very small steps make success.
label: founder_execution
interpretation: He presents incremental hiring, revenue, and operating progress as the building blocks of success, indicating an appreciation for steady execution without establishing a hard investment threshold.

quote:
Doing one thing well has been, I think, one of the things I tell entrepreneurs the most.
Here we go.
Okay.
The facts are, so many entrepreneurs start businesses and they like to do things all over the place.
They say, look at how amazing this is, and then they say, and I got something else.
That never really works well.
label: product_success_factor_assessment
interpretation: His advice emphasizes concentrated product or company focus and treats simultaneous pursuit of disparate offerings as a recurring execution weakness; it remains operating advice rather than an explicit investment preference.

quote:
you can only really do one thing well.
And so if you're maniacally focused on doing one thing well,
you'll probably do great.
When I see entrepreneurs trying to do five things well,
they don't actually do well.
label: founder_execution
interpretation: Hyatt associates founder focus with stronger execution and views excessive simultaneous priorities negatively, though he does not frame this as a mechanical screening rule.

quote:
We actually need to produce tons and tons of people in high tech in this country.
We're going to be left behind because the future of technology is exponential.
It's not linear, and it's going to crush a lot of industries.
label: market_timing
interpretation: This historical forecast expresses Hyatt's view that accelerating technological change creates urgency around high-tech capacity, but it neither verifies present conditions nor establishes a sector investment mandate.

quote:
we just a general purpose investing so i spend my time
looking at deals and meeting new people and hearing very interesting things.
label: investment_thesis_constraint
interpretation: Hyatt describes his investing activity as general-purpose rather than identifying a narrow mandate; the statement does not establish specific stage, sector, geography, or check-size parameters.

quote:
And I think starting companies at terrible times is a really good idea because essentially
you're ignored by competitors.
There's a lack of competition.
You have time to kind of get your business going.
label: market_timing
interpretation: From his operating experience, Hyatt argues that downturns can create favorable company-building conditions by reducing competitive pressure; this is operating advice rather than a stated investment mandate.

quote:
So we just bootstrapped it in the beginning, which was incredibly beneficial to us later
when we sold the company.
Because most people start a company and give up like 40% of the company in the first two
years, and we never did that.
So it was great on our exit.
label: founder_equity_incentive_alignment
interpretation: Hyatt's operating history makes him favorable toward early capital efficiency and preserving founder ownership, though he does not state a mechanical ownership threshold for investments.

quote:
Listen, whenever you start a company, you should be in your mindset.
I'm going to be in this thing for 10 to 20 years.
And that's how you should see a company.
label: founder_motivation_authenticity
interpretation: His advice favors founders approaching company-building as a long-term commitment, but it does not establish a formal investment-duration requirement.

quote:
Well, as you start generating revenue and showing that clients buy your product,
and not only buy your product, buy more of your product.
you're de-risking the deal, you're increasing your valuation.
Most people expect to raise money before they de-risk the deal in any way.
label: traction_repeatability_concern
interpretation: Hyatt explicitly treats revenue, initial purchases, and expansion purchases as evidence that reduces investment risk and supports valuation.

quote:
If you just have a minimum viable product,
you just put it out there.
You don't really have clients.
You just have a bunch of smart guys and girls doing some stuff.
I'll say that's amazing,
but I'm not sure you have a company.
label: traction_repeatability_concern
interpretation: He explicitly regards an MVP and capable builders without customers as insufficient evidence that a viable company has been established.

quote:
Because you're not the decider.
I'm not the decider.
The only decider that matters.
Is the client saying, I want this?
And I'll buy it and I'll buy more of it.
label: product_adoption
interpretation: Hyatt identifies customers' willingness to purchase and expand purchases as the decisive validation signal.

quote:
I like B2B.
Listen, some people can come in and build...
you know, the Airbnb type companies or the, you know, food dashing companies and all this kind
of stuff. And they're great at it. I'm not.
label: business_model_assessment
interpretation: Hyatt directly expresses a personal preference and capability fit for B2B businesses over consumer marketplace-style companies, without claiming a binding mandate.

quote:
When you're doing B2C, you have to be in it to win it, and you have to raise a tremendous amount of money, and you have to get over a velocity.
So, you know, when you see Uber and Lyft be successful, you haven't seen the 80,000 companies that just couldn't do it.
You know, because the amount of money that Uber and Lyft have literally drunk to get
to where it's an insatiable appetite of capital flow.
And if you can't keep up with that, you can't do it.
label: capital_intensity_concern
interpretation: He explicitly views many B2C businesses as requiring unusually large and sustained capital commitments to reach sufficient scale, creating material financing risk.

quote:
The only thing...
I can assure you that luck does play a part of entrepreneurship, but the number one thing that
defines entrepreneurs is literal perseverance. And even if you persevere, it doesn't mean you're
going to make it.
label: founder_qualities
interpretation: Hyatt emphasizes perseverance as a central entrepreneurial trait while acknowledging that it does not guarantee success; this is founder advice rather than an explicit screening rule.

quote:
you have to whatever your plan is it's going to cost more and take longer it's kind of like building a house
and you're just going to be wrong. You're going to be told everything you've said about the
finances of your company are going to be wrong. I don't know which way you're wrong, but you're
probably going to be wrong. Your hockey stick is not going to work out.
label: growth_projection_risk
interpretation: His operating advice reflects skepticism toward precise cost, timing, financial, and hockey-stick projections, suggesting plans should be assessed with substantial uncertainty rather than treated as reliable forecasts.

quote:
The digital transformation that would have naturally happened over seven to 10 years
is happening in one year because it has to.
And you're a product of it.
You're seeing it.
label: market_timing
interpretation: This is a historical, undated prediction made during the pandemic that digital adoption was accelerating sharply; it may explain contemporaneous market enthusiasm but is not verified as a current thesis.

quote:
Those are all great questions. I think that I make investments to build a business with
entrepreneurs I really like and I want to be in business with for 10 years.
I don't give people money that I don't like.
I don't give people money that I don't believe in.
label: founder_qualities
interpretation: Hyatt explicitly places personal regard, belief in the entrepreneur, and willingness to sustain a decade-long relationship at the center of his investment selection.

quote:
I don't find brilliant a-holes.
I just don't do it.
label: founder_qualities
interpretation: He explicitly rejects investing solely on brilliance when the founder's character makes them an undesirable long-term partner.

quote:
The only thing that matters to me in my life today is my time.
Because every minute I spend doing this, I'm not with my daughter.
I'm not with my family.
So I've got to choose.
label: decision_context_constraint
interpretation: His opportunity cost of time creates a strong personal constraint on investment selection and involvement.

quote:
So I invest to build, to back an entrepreneur or entrepreneurs, brothers or sisters or whatever.
And I back them so they can build a big company, hire a bunch of people, make a difference and do something great.
If you don't want to do something great, then I'm not your partner.
label: founder_investor_vision_alignment
interpretation: He seeks founders whose ambition to build a large, consequential company aligns with his own desired direction for the partnership.

quote:
There's many companies I don't fund, which I find them good people, good idea, good whatever.
But I'm not going to commit my time to it.
I've committed my time to two or three entrepreneurs and two or three businesses where I sit on
the board, I give my time, I give my opinion, and I lean in.
And it's worked out tremendously well.
label: investor_value_add_fit
interpretation: He favors a small number of opportunities where he is willing to contribute substantial board-level time and advice; merely liking the people or idea is insufficient.

quote:
And I brought in my money.
And there's times when I can do the whole round on my own,
but I pull back and I bring in my friends who can also help.
label: investor_value_add_fit
interpretation: Even when able to finance an entire round, he may syndicate with people who can provide additional help to the company.

quote:
I'm actually not out there looking for deal flow.
I don't have a fund.
I don't have my, I have a family office.
It's me and my brother and some great partners
that help me do stuff and place money.
If I don't do another deal and for 10 years, I don't care.
label: fund_economics_constraint
interpretation: He describes investing through a family office rather than a fund and therefore lacking pressure to source or complete new deals on a fixed cadence.

quote:
I mean, I invest in funds and venture capital firms and private equity and real estate.
I'm only in it to win it if I really like the people and I want to back them and I want
to have a decade of conversations with them.
That's a very high bar.
label: founder_qualities
interpretation: For direct entrepreneurial backing, he explicitly applies a high bar centered on liking the people and wanting an enduring relationship, while also noting broader investment activity across several asset types.

quote:
Amazing. I'm very bullish about the future. I think it just gets better and better.
I think the world is getting dramatically better. I think despite COVID and despite what you see in
political systems and everything that you're seeing in the planet, I think the world is
getting much, much better. I think the fake news that it's not. And I just think this pandemic
will pass. We will get past it. And out of these ashes, you'll see so many great entrepreneurs
rise. I think it's never been a better time to start a business. It's never been a better time
to be an entrepreneur. I just think you're overwhelmed with a lot of clickbait.
label: market_timing
interpretation: In this historically situated pandemic-era forecast, he expressed broad optimism about company formation and expected strong entrepreneurs to emerge from the disruption; it does not establish a current sector or timing mandate.

quote:
It's actually Moore's Law is happening to you right in front of you.
And you don't even know it.
label: market_timing
interpretation: Hyatt portrays exponential improvements in computing as an underrecognized technology shift, suggesting historical optimism about opportunities arising during rapid capability growth.

quote:
In 1990, it cost us $3 billion to sequence the human genome.
Today,
It's 10 bucks.
3 billion, 10 bucks.
3 billion, 10 bucks.
That's faster than exponential.
label: solution_feasibility_assessment
interpretation: The example emphasizes dramatic cost compression as a force that can make previously impractical technological applications feasible; it is an operating observation rather than an explicit investment criterion.

quote:
So let me tell you, it smells like internet 1994 again.
Do you know what internet 1994 smells like?
You know it's gonna be big,
you know something's going on,
but you just don't know what.
label: market_timing
interpretation: Hyatt compares the technology environment to an early, consequential internet era, indicating historical enthusiasm about a large but still uncertain emerging opportunity.

quote:
We haven't even seen the warm up act
yet for artificial intelligence.
We haven't even seen the warm up act of what's coming.
label: market_timing
interpretation: This is a historically stated forecast that artificial intelligence remained at an early point in its development, not evidence of a formal sector mandate or a verified current prediction.
